newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon minister fears cocoa sector shrinkage.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon minister fears cocoa sector shrinkage.

text.p: Cameroon cocoa and coffee farmers may quit plantations for good this year after diving prices and quality in 1995/96 followed earlier market reforms, its Agriculture Minister said.
"At the moment there are doubts whether production of cocoa and coffee will pick up again," Agriculture Minister Frederic Kodock told a year-end review meeting last week.
"We are afraid that farmers may completely abandon their cocoa and coffee plantations to move to more lucrative agricultural products," he added.
Average prices have fallen to 340 CFA per kg from 495 per kg over the year.
"The cocoa economy is very fragile," he added.

Buyers on the whole paid less in areas where there were more producers, with prices ranging from 300-400 CFA per kilo in the central area, 400 CFA in the east and 400-700 in the south, west, southwest and along the coast. The FOB export price for cocoa last week stood at 724 CFA per kilo.
Cocoa production increased to 130,000 tonnes in 1995/96 from 109,000 tonnes in 1994/95, but Cameroon has acknowledged drastically falling quality, Kodock added.

Its cocoa quality slipped from "good" to "fair" quality listing at London's LIFFE (then LCE) commodity exchange after 1991 when donor-sponsored free-market reforms abolished upcountry quality checks and relaxed export control measures.
Earlier this year large amounts of cocoa were believed to have been smuggled to neighbouring Nigeria, where prices were higher.

Cameroon closed its National Produce Marketing Board in 1991 and replaced it with the National Cocoa and Coffee Board to liberalise the sector. Inexperienced intermediaries took over marketing and exporter numbers jumped from 40 in the late 1980s to around 200 today.

"With the closure of the National Produce Marketing Board it became difficult for farmers to get regular supplies of pesticide," said Kodock, commenting on quality. Before the closure, subsidised and regular supplies had been available.
Cameroon's cocoa and coffee board chief Hope Sona Ebai in December put 1996/97 production at about 120,000 tonnes which he wanted repeated until 1999 to meet world (ICCO) output targets.
The World Bank and International Monetary Fund have linked cocoa sector reforms to loan deals with several other West African countries with state-controlled marketing agencies.
Advice includes ending state monopoly over buying and exports, scrapping commission and producer price fixing and instead recommending farmers minimum, not imposing fixed prices.
In Nigeria as well as Cameroon numerous inexperienced firms sprang up after liberalisation and this, coupled with relaxed controls, led to lower bean quality and loss of premium payments.

The tiny West African cocoa producer, Togo, was the latest to cut its state marketing body's role in December 1996. Ghana and the world's largest producer, Ivory Coast, have also implemented a mix of internal and external marketing reforms.

Ghana Cocoa Board chief John Henry Newman said in December new cocoa quality monitoring equipment would be in place in 4-5 months at ports in an effort to secure the country's premium quality sale prices.
